data.name: All Our Asias
data.detailed_description:
In this free 3D adventure, explore someone's mind and discover their secrets in a surreal story about a father, son, Asian-America and more. Explore a dying father's "Memory World", and travel to familiar, supernatural spaces. By Melos, co-creator of Anodyne and Angeline Era.

The protagonist is Yuito. 31, Japanese-American. Hedge fund analyst. One day he receives a letter from his estranged father, who is dying. It's too late for Yuito to speak to him. But, his father is on life support, so Yuito has an opportunity. He can under go a Memory World Visitation, and enter his father's Memory World - supernatural landscapes where Yuito can explore his father's experiences and secrets. It is risky, Yuito feels compelled to make the journey... 

Be sure to buy the $4.99 Fan Pack, which contains the hour-long OST and an exclusive 150+ page artbook containing commentary on the art, music, story and more!

  • 90-120+ minutes long.

  • Navigate surreal and ''realistic'' areas via simple 3rd-person movement and light platforming. Easy to play.

  • Converse with characters small and large as Yuito progresses deeper into this Memory World.

  • A lo-fi art direction influenced by the PSX and N64 era.

  • A soundtrack by Melos Han-Tani, and talented collaborators.

  • From Melos Han-Tani, the co-creator of Anodyne and Even the Ocean.

Additional Credits:

Logo: Alex Van Dorp

Yuito Portrait Art: Ray Chen (Linework), Marina Kittaka (Color)

In-game "navigation UI": Marina Kittaka

Box Art: Marina Kittaka

Guest OST Composers: EQUIP (#25), kynes (#18), _zebra (#21), Bryant Canelo (#16)

reviews.review:
All Our Asias is a very strange game, but in a way that I think works surprisingly well. I play as Yuito, a Japanese American man whose father is dying, and I enter a strange Memory World built from his father's memories. From there I am exploring surreal places, talking to characters and trying to understand more about a father Yuito never really knew. It is a very short experience, around 90 minutes to two hours, and it feels much more like a personal story than a traditional adventure game.

The thing I like most is the atmosphere. Everything has this strange old 3D look that reminds me of early PlayStation and N64 games, but the simple graphics actually fit the dreamlike setting really well. The environments can look familiar one moment and completely bizarre the next, which makes exploring the Memory World feel like I am moving through someone's thoughts rather than a normal game world. The music also adds a lot to this. It is calm and sometimes quite haunting, and it gives the whole experience a feeling that is difficult to get from a more conventional adventure game.

The story is where most of the real substance is for me. Yuito is trying to understand his father, but the game also gets into ideas about Asian American identity, family, race, immigration and the way people can inherit experiences they never personally lived through. I like that it does not simply give me a straightforward explanation of everything. A lot of the meaning comes from the strange places I visit and the conversations I have along the way. It can feel confusing at times, but that confusion also suits the idea of exploring somebody else's memories.

There is not much traditional gameplay here. I am mostly walking around, talking to characters and doing some light platforming, with some sections involving a small flying vehicle. There are also secrets and optional things I can discover, which gives me a little reason to look around instead of simply following the most obvious route. Still, I have to be honest about what this game is. I am not getting combat, complicated puzzles or a deep progression system. The gameplay exists mainly to let me experience the story and the world, so I think it works much better when I treat it as a short interactive story rather than expecting a full RPG.

The short length is probably the biggest weakness for me. I actually think the game benefits from not overstaying its welcome, because the unusual ideas would probably lose some of their impact if they were stretched across a huge campaign. At the same time, I finished feeling like there was still more that could have been explored. Some of the story moves in directions that feel quite sudden, and there are ideas that I would have liked to spend more time with. The simple movement and camera can also feel a little awkward, especially when I am trying to navigate some of the more open areas.

I do appreciate how personal the whole project feels. The developer deliberately presents the game as an authored work, and that makes the strange structure and unusual subject matter feel much more intentional. It is not trying to be another generic adventure game with a serious story attached to it. It has its own voice, its own visual style and its own way of discussing identity and family. I also like that it is completely free, because I can experience the whole story without needing to make a big commitment or spend anything.

Overall, All Our Asias is a short and unusual experience that I think is much more interesting for its ideas and atmosphere than its actual gameplay. I like the surreal memory world, the strange old school graphics, the music and especially the story about Yuito trying to understand his dying father and his own identity. The basic movement can feel clunky and the short length means there is not a huge amount of gameplay, but I do not think this game needs to be long to make its point. For me, it is the kind of game I remember because of how different it feels rather than because of any particular mechanic.

Rating: 7.7/10
